On GET, on a refused post and for the post's own validation, the page's form is the Validator's, so the page offers the choices the Validator accepts:

class OfferedAuthorsForm(BookForm):
    """``BookForm``, offering the authors its constructor is handed."""

    def __init__(self, *args: Any, authors: QuerySet[Author], **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.fields["author"].queryset = authors


def offered_authors(*, user: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
    # Staff add a book by anyone; everyone else by an author already shelved.
    authors = Author.objects.all()
    if not user.is_staff:
        authors = authors.filter(books__isnull=False).distinct()
    return {"authors": authors}


shelve_book_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=add_book,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=FormValidator(OfferedAuthorsForm, form_kwargs=offered_authors),
)

The URLconf routes it as books/shelve/. A signed-in user who is not staff is offered only the authors already on the shelves, and a post naming another is refused on the author field; staff are offered every author.

docs.title: A partial page
docs.text:
A partial spec gets the same page, built on the same form. The page's form renders no HTML required attribute, so the browser sends a post that leaves a field blank, and a blank field is absent, as it is on every page: on a partial call, a field the operation leaves as it is. A post with every field blank dispatches with no arguments but what a checkbox or a multi-select always sends, and the page does not refuse it.

# The same update as a partial one: a field left blank is left as it is.
change_book_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=edit_book,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=book_validator,
    instance_selector_spec=edit_book_spec.instance_selector_spec,
    partial=True,
)

The URLconf routes it as books/<int:pk>/change/: a post with the title left blank and a new price changes the price and keeps the title.

A blank field cannot clear a value there, since blank means "leave it": a partial operation that clears a value needs a field of its own that says so, as an optional file's clear checkbox does. A checkbox and a multi-select are always sent, ticked or not, so each is written as posted. And beside a shape-check refusal, a partial page's form carries the refusal alone: its Validator takes the fields a post leaves out off its own form, and the page's form, validated whole, would call each blank field required.

as_view() refuses, when the URLconf is imported, a view with no ServiceSpec, a spec whose Validator is not a FormValidator, a many spec, whose list of rows no form posts, and a view with neither a success_url nor its own get_success_url; then every check the JSON views make of the request's hooks, below. The view is sync only in this release.

docs.title: What the page acts on
docs.text:
The page shows its target, the row or set the operation acts on, in the context beside the form, on GET and on every refused post it re-renders, the fragment included:

Key Holds Present target the row an instance_selector_spec found, or the set a collection_selector_spec resolved wherever there is a target: absent for a create, and for a missing row allow_none lets through target_count how many rows the set holds for a set target_counted_at when it counted them, django.utils.timezone.now() for a set target_display the target as a person reads it, below on a page that sets display_target

A key with nothing to hold is absent rather than None, as unavailable is.

@dataclasses.dataclass
class BookOut:
    """A book as an operation returns it, and as its page names it."""

    pk: Annotated[int, FieldMarking.handle()]  # another call's input: never shown
    title: Annotated[str, FieldMarking.label()]  # the name a page calls it by
    price: Decimal
    status: Status  # spoken as its display: "Draft", not "draft"
    published_on: Annotated[datetime.date | None, FieldMarking.hidden()]


class WithdrawForm(forms.Form):
    reason = forms.CharField(max_length=200)


def withdraw(*, instance: Book, data: dict[str, Any]) -> Book:
    instance.status = Status.DRAFT
    instance.save(update_fields=["status"])
    return instance


# One book: the page shows it, by its title, beside the form.
withdraw_book_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=withdraw,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=FormValidator(WithdrawForm),
    instance_selector_spec=edit_book_spec.instance_selector_spec,
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(BookOut),
)


class PublishForm(forms.Form):
    published_on = forms.DateField()


def drafts() -> QuerySet[Book]:
    return Book.objects.filter(status=Status.DRAFT).order_by("title")


def publish(*, collection: QuerySet[Book], data: dict[str, Any]) -> list[int]:
    published = list(collection.values_list("pk", flat=True))
    collection.update(status=Status.PUBLISHED, published_on=data["published_on"])
    return published


# Every draft at once: the page counts the set, and names the first few.
publish_drafts_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=publish,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=FormValidator(PublishForm),
    collection_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(kind=SelectorKind.LIST, selector=drafts),
    output_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
        selector=lambda *, result: Book.objects.filter(pk__in=result).order_by("title"),
        presenter=DataclassPresenter(BookOut),
    ),
)

The URLconf routes the first as books/<int:pk>/withdraw/ and the second as books/publish-drafts/, with target_display_limit=3, both with display_target=True and both rendering this template:

{% if target_count is not None %}
  <p>{{ target_count }} book{{ target_count|pluralize }} selected, counted at {{ target_counted_at|time:"H:i" }}.</p>
  {% if target_display %}
    <ul>{% for book in target_display %}<li>{{ book.label }}</li>{% endfor %}</ul>
    {% if target_count > target_display|length %}<p>The first {{ target_display|length }} are shown.</p>{% endif %}
  {% endif %}
{% elif target_display %}
  <h1>{{ target_display.label }}</h1>
  <dl>{% for name, value in target_display.pairs %}<dt>{{ name }}</dt><dd>{{ value }}</dd>{% endfor %}</dl>
{% endif %}
<form method="post">{% csrf_token %}{{ form }}<button name="save">Save</button></form>

docs.title: A bulk page
docs.text:
A spec with a collection_selector_spec acts on a set, and its page says how many rows the set holds. An empty set is no refusal: its scope check is still asked, there is no not-found exit, and the page above says "0 books selected" where an instance page answers 404. A queryset is counted with a COUNT on a fresh clone of it, so no row is read to count it; a set a selector answers as a list is counted with len().

The count is a time-of-check, not a promise. The rows may change between the page and its post, so the context carries when the set was counted, and a template says "5 books selected, counted at 14:02" rather than "5 books will be published". The post does not replay what the page counted: it re-runs the service on the set it finds then, and a refused post counts the set again. A successful post counts nothing. So nothing about the count belongs in a hidden input.

docs.title: The target's display
docs.text:
A page that sets display_target = True shows its target as a person reads it, under target_display. It is off by default, because the FieldMarkings it reads are on the spec's Output - its own presenter's, or its output_selector_spec's - and an Output describes what the operation returns, which need not be its target: a withdrawal may return a receipt. A page whose Output is marked serves as it did until it opts in, and asks no presenter. On:

  • the target is presented through that presenter, handed the context dispatch hands it: the principal, the target, the request's one call context, and the call's seeds as ambient;
  • then projected by the kernel's project_payload: a HIDDEN field is dropped, and a choice is spoken as its display;
  • and every HANDLE is dropped as well, at any depth. An agent keeps a handle to pass to another tool, and a person is never shown one.

A row's display is a dict: its fields, the same fields as pairs of name and value in order, and label, the value of the field marked LABEL, where one is. Loop over pairs rather than fields.items: a template looks the key items up before the method, so an Output with a field of that name would loop over its value. Above, the book is named "The Lathe of Heaven" and its fields are its title, its price and its status, read as "Published": the key is a handle and the publication date is hidden. A set's display is a list of those, one per row, for at most target_display_limit rows, 10 by default: the first that many in the set's own order, read by one query bounded by a LIMIT, and presented by one call of the presenter's presented_rows(). target_count still counts every row, so a template can say how many it left out. as_view() refuses a target_display_limit that is not a positive int, a bool included.

as_view() refuses a page displaying its target, when the URLconf is imported, where its spec has no Output, where the Output marks none of its own fields - choices alone are not markings, and nor is a marking only inside a nested object - and where the kernel's projection refuses the markings, such as two fields marked LABEL. What it cannot check is whether the Output describes the target's rows, since that is known only once one is presented: an Output that does not raises on the page's first request. That is the cost of turning the display on. A bulk operation whose service returns something else re-reads its rows with an output_selector_spec, as publish_drafts_spec does. The raw target stays beside the display, for a template that wants both.

docs.title: The confirmation page
docs.text:
A service that finds it needs one more value asks for it by raising AdditionalInputRequired with a schema keyed by the argument it wants back, and the page renders that question: the form again, bound to every value the post carried, with the field that answers it revealed. The answer comes back as an ordinary field of the next post, so there is nothing to hold between the two and no session to resume.

class DiscardForm(forms.Form):
    reason = forms.CharField(max_length=200, required=False)
    # The answer to the service's question, declared like any other field:
    # the page holds it back until the question asks for it.
    confirmed = forms.BooleanField(required=False, label="Yes, discard them")


def discard(*, collection: QuerySet[Book], data: dict[str, Any]) -> list[int]:
    if not data["confirmed"]:
        raise AdditionalInputRequired(
            f"{collection.count()} drafts will be deleted. Confirm to proceed.",
            schema={"confirmed": {"type": "boolean"}},
        )
    discarded = list(collection.values_list("pk", flat=True))
    collection.delete()
    return discarded


# Every draft, deleted once a person says yes.
discard_drafts_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=discard,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=FormValidator(DiscardForm),
    collection_selector_spec=publish_drafts_spec.collection_selector_spec,
    output_selector_spec=publish_drafts_spec.output_selector_spec,
)

The answer is a field the spec's form declares, here confirmed: an optional BooleanField, whose box left unticked cleans to False. The page builds no widget from the schema, because the closed argument set refuses a key no parameter declares, so a control the form does not declare could never carry the answer. asked_fields holds the field back until a question names it. It is taken out of the form every GET and every other refusal renders, so {{ form }}, or a template rendering fields one by one, shows no box, and a box never shown posts nothing: the service reads False and asks. as_view() refuses asked_fields unless it is a tuple of the form's own fields, each optional, since a field held back is absent from every post no question asked for, none the form disables, since a disabled field is never read from a post, and none a server_arguments binding answers for. A held field a refusal's error names is shown with its error.

The URLconf routes it as books/discard-drafts/, with display_target=True and asked_fields=("confirmed",), through this template and a page that includes it, named as the fragment_template_name:

<form method="post" hx-post="" hx-swap="outerHTML">{% csrf_token %}
  <p>{{ target_count }} draft{{ target_count|pluralize }} selected, counted at {{ target_counted_at|time:"H:i" }}.</p>
  <ul>{% for book in target_display %}<li>{{ book.label }}</li>{% endfor %}</ul>
  {{ form }}
  <button name="save">{% if requested_input %}Discard them{% else %}Discard{% endif %}</button>
</form>

What a post that is asked gets back:

  • The kernel's check_requested_input reads the schema first, with the request's seeds. A question no route could hear answered - a key no parameter declares, one a seed fills, a shape a transport cannot render, a type the parameter would refuse - raises ImproperlyConfigured out of the view, on the page and in the fragment alike, rather than being rendered. It is the service's mistake, and the JSON views raise it too.
  • The page answers 422, the map's status, and the fragment 200, in place: the form's own target, with no HX-Retarget or HX-Reswap.
  • The form is re-rendered with the boxes the schema names revealed, every other value as it was posted, and the message among its non-field errors, as any other refusal's. A box asked for again after a yes is shown empty, so one click never answers a question nobody read.
  • The context carries requested_input, absent on every other answer:
Key Holds requested_input.message the refusal's message requested_input.schema the schema it asked under, or None requested_input.fields the form's bound fields the schema names, in its order

A key the schema names that no field of the form declares, such as a parameter the spec reads from the route, is asked by its message alone.

The page that asks counts again. On a bulk page the set is counted for the post that asked, after the service's pass, so target_count and target_counted_at say what the confirming post will find as of then, not what the GET counted: above, a draft added between the page and its post makes the question say "3 drafts". The confirming post re-runs the service on the set as it is when it arrives, and is asked again if the service finds a reason to.

docs.title: A confirmation that lands elsewhere
docs.text:
A form in a table row whose question needs a dialog puts the dialog in the spec-form fragment as an out-of-band element, which htmx swaps into the element of the same id wherever it is on the page, beside the form swapped in place. The view's Python does not change, and it sets no header:

<html>
<body>
<h1>Drafts</h1>
{% if not requested_input %}<dialog id="confirm-discard"></dialog>{% endif %}
{% partialdef spec-form inline %}
<form id="discard-drafts" method="post" hx-post="" hx-swap="outerHTML">
  {% csrf_token %}
  {% if not requested_input %}{{ form.non_field_errors }}{% endif %}
  {% for field in form %}{% if not requested_input or field.name not in requested_input.schema %}
    {{ field.errors }}{{ field.label_tag }} {{ field }}
  {% endif %}{% endfor %}
  <button name="save">Discard</button>
</form>
{% if requested_input %}
<dialog id="confirm-discard" hx-swap-oob="true" open>
  <p>{{ requested_input.message }}</p>
  {% for field in requested_input.fields %}
  <label><input type="checkbox" name="{{ field.html_name }}" form="discard-drafts"> {{ field.label }}</label>
  {% endfor %}
  <button name="save" form="discard-drafts">Discard them</button>
</dialog>
{% endif %}
{% endpartialdef %}
</body>
</html>

The URLconf routes it as books/discard-drafts/in-a-dialog/. Every field of the form but the ones asked for is rendered in the form, and the dialog carries the message, the box and a button. They sit outside the form, so each names it with HTML's form attribute, which is what makes them post with it; a control outside the form with no form attribute posts nothing. The page renders the empty dialog only before a question, so whichever way the page is rendered there is one element with its id. An id that matches no element on the page swaps nothing.

docs.title: Not a gate on an agent route
docs.text: The question is a page's affordance, never a security boundary. On an agent route, the same AdditionalInputRequired goes back to the model as a retry naming the missing argument, and the model can answer confirmed: true itself on its next call, with nobody asked. So nothing that must have a person's yes may rely on this question. For a human gate on an agent route, enable ToolGuard in django-spec-agents, whose approval card a person answers before the tool runs, and keep the spec's tool out of its exempt list.

docs.title: What the request carries
docs.text:
The page reads the request as the JSON views do, with the same attributes and hooks, checked by the same code:

  • route_kwargs says which URL kwargs fill which parameters, a mapping to rename or drop ({"branch": None}) or a tuple of names to allow, as on SpecView. as_view() refuses a bare string and a target or an allowed name the spec does not declare, and two kwargs filling one parameter are refused on the request that captures both.
  • get_pool_seeds(request), pool_seeds unless overridden, answers the seeds this request's call is resolved with. It is asked once per request, and every step that resolves a spec callable is handed what it answered: the target's lookup and its object-level or scope check, the affordances below, the form's form_kwargs, and dispatch. Seed what the request carries, never the request itself. The class-level check is asked with them too: the page asks has_permission before it reads anything else, through the kernel's authorize, which resolves the seeds the check names, so a check reading a tenant admits the principal on the page as dispatch would.
  • get_server_arguments(request), server_arguments unless overridden, answers the kernel's ServerArguments, and three readers of the call read the server's value for each name it answers for: the page's form, the target's lookup and dispatch. A field of the page's form that the binding binds renders disabled, showing the server's value; one it withholds renders disabled and empty, on GET and on a refused post alike, so the page never shows a value the client posted for it. A disabled field is not read from the post, so a value the client was never offered is never coerced or refused; the binding is laid over the post's arguments before dispatch, and over the route's before the target is found, so a target selector reading a bound parameter finds the row by the server's value. Anything else a template shows - the row's own fields, say - is what it is.

A named seed is resolved again at each step that names it, because the Grant a step hands on carries no values. On a POST, the class-level check, the target's lookup and dispatch each resolve it, and the form's keywords too where form_kwargs names it; on a GET, the affordances' pool takes dispatch's place, and a target's display, where the page shows one, is presented with that same pool. A refused post that presents a display resolves it once more, for the presenter's. So a resolver answering a fresh object answers each step a different one. Write seed resolvers that answer the same each time.

One call context per request. The page creates one plain dict for each request, starting with request, this request, and view, this page, and hands that same object to every kernel call it makes: the class-level check, the target's lookup and its object-level or scope check, the affordances, the form's form_kwargs and dispatch. So a check, a condition, form_kwargs or the service declaring call_context reads what an earlier stage of the same request put there, and each request gets a dict of its own. A selector, a check, a condition, a seed's resolver, form_kwargs or the service naming request or view is handed the one in it, as on the JSON views, and the display's presenter reads the page's seeds as its ambient, never the context.

The checks are the JSON views': as_view() refuses an async def hook, checks server_arguments with the kernel's check_server_arguments against the declared pool_seeds, and refuses a route_kwargs filling a name the binding answers for. On each request, a per-call binding that binds or withholds other names than the declared one, a seed added per call under a bound or withheld name, and a route capture filling a name the server answers for are each refused as ImproperlyConfigured, the last pointing at route_kwargs={name: None}.

BRANCHES = {"main", "harbour"}
CLOSED_BRANCHES = {"harbour"}


class AtABranch(PermissionCheck):
    message = "There is no such branch."

    def has_permission(self, principal: Any, spec: Any, *, branch: str) -> bool:
        # A seed, named by the class-level check: the page asks it with the
        # one get_pool_seeds adds, before it offers the form.
        return branch in BRANCHES


def branch_open(*, branch: str) -> bool:
    # ``branch`` is a seed, so every transport serving this spec seeds its own.
    return branch not in CLOSED_BRANCHES


stock_book_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=add_book,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn(), AtABranch()],
    validator=book_validator,
    affordances=[
        Affordance(
            code="branch_closed",
            reason="This branch is closed for stocktaking.",
            when=branch_open,
        ),
    ],
)


class StockBook(SpecFormView):
    spec = stock_book_spec
    template_name = "spec_form_available.html"
    success_url = reverse_lazy("books")
    # Every route under ``branches/<branch>/`` captures ``branch``, which this
    # spec reads as a seed rather than an argument: drop it, and hold every
    # other kwarg strict.
    route_kwargs = {"branch": None}
    # A book stocked at a branch starts as a draft, whatever the form posts:
    # the status field renders disabled, and the posted value is dropped.
    server_arguments = ServerArguments(values={"status": Status.DRAFT})

    def get_pool_seeds(self, request: HttpRequest) -> PoolSeeds:
        # What the request carries, never the request itself.
        return self.pool_seeds.extend(branch=lambda: self.kwargs["branch"])

The URLconf routes it as branches/<branch>/books/new/. AtABranch, a class-level check, names the branch seed, so a branch it does not know is PermissionDenied on GET and on POST before the form is built. Its status renders disabled with draft selected, and a posted status is dropped: every book it adds is a draft.

docs.title: An operation that is unavailable
docs.text:
A spec's Affordance conditions say whether the operation is possible right now, and the page asks them on GET, after it has found the target, so it never offers a form whose post the spec would refuse at 409:

  • The callable conditions are asked always, through the kernel's unmet_operation_affordance, on a pool base_pool builds from the call's own seeds. So a condition reading a seed get_pool_seeds adds, as branch_open above reads branch, is asked with it.
  • When the target is a row and every callable condition is met, the conditions on the row are asked too, as dispatch asks them. A target of None - a create, or a missing row allow_none lets through - is no row, and no row condition is asked about it.
  • The first unmet one is in the context as unavailable: the Affordance itself, whose code and reason a template reads. When every condition is met, unavailable is absent from the context, not None. The fragment renders from the same context, so an hx-get that loads the form carries it too.

Every callable condition is asked twice on a GET with a row: once alone, then again with the row's conditions, since the kernel's enforce_affordances asks them all as dispatch does. Each seed is resolved twice as well, once for the target's lookup and once for the affordances' pool, and once more for each of the class-level check and the form's form_kwargs that names it. Write conditions and seed resolvers that may be asked more than once and answer the same.

The callable conditions are asked first, without a row, so where both kinds are unmet and the row's is declared first, the page names the callable while the post is refused with the row's: dispatch asks in declaration order. The page's answer is advice, and the post's refusal is the authority: the POST is unchanged, dispatch asks every condition again, and a condition that changed between the two requests is answered by the 409.

A refused post carries the refusal's code in its context, beside the form, for a refusal that has one: ActionUnavailable, whose code is the one the JSON body carries beside its detail. It is absent for every other refusal. The fragment's context carries it too, so a template branches on the stable code rather than on the message.

There is no default template yet, so a host's template says it:

{% if unavailable %}<p class="unavailable" data-code="{{ unavailable.code }}">{{ unavailable.reason }}</p>{% endif %}
<form method="post">{% csrf_token %}
  {% if code == "branch_closed" %}<p class="next"><a href="/branches/">Choose another branch.</a></p>{% endif %}
  <fieldset{% if unavailable %} disabled{% endif %}>{{ form }}<button name="save">Save</button></fieldset>
</form>

On the closed branch above, the page says why and disables the form, and a post made anyway comes back at 409 with the reason among the form's errors and the link to another branch beside it.

docs.title: An htmx request
docs.text:
Turning htmx on is a template change. The view answers every request with the page unless htmx asked for less, and then answers the same outcome with the part of the page the request swaps, rendered from the same template. Wrap the page's form in {% partialdef spec-form inline %}, give the form hx-post and a target, and, for a success answered in place, define spec-result:

<html>
<body>
<h1>New book</h1>
{% partialdef spec-form inline %}
<form method="post" hx-post="{% url 'add-book' %}" hx-swap="outerHTML">
  {% csrf_token %}{{ form }}<button name="save">Save</button>
</form>
{% endpartialdef %}
{% partialdef spec-result %}
<p id="saved">Added {{ result.value.title }}.</p>
{% endpartialdef %}
</body>
</html>

urlpatterns = [
    # The same view as a plain page: only the template changed.
    path(
        "books/new/",
        SpecFormView.as_view(
            spec=add_book_spec,
            template_name="spec_form_htmx.html",
            success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
        ),
        name="add-book",
    ),
    path("books/", books, name="books"),
]

The view's Python does not change: inline renders the form where it stands on the page, and the same block is addressable on its own as spec_form_htmx.html#spec-form, which is where the view looks for it by default. The tag and that #name address are Django 6.0's. Below 6.0, install django-template-partials (23.3 or later, the first with partialdef) and configure it in TEMPLATES: its tag as a builtin, and its loader around the project's own.

# settings.py, below Django 6.0 only: from 6.0 Django has the tag and the
# address itself, and this would register a second partialdef over its own.
TEMPLATES = [
    {
        "BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates",
        "DIRS": [BASE_DIR / "templates"],
        "OPTIONS": {
            # The tag as a builtin, so the page's template needs no
            # {% load partials %}, which Django 6.0 would not find.
            "builtins": ["template_partials.templatetags.partials"],
            # Its loader around the project's own, for the page.html#name
            # address. Adding "template_partials" to INSTALLED_APPS sets this
            # one up for you, and the builtin above still has to be named.
            "loaders": [
                (
                    "template_partials.loader.Loader",
                    [
                        "django.template.loaders.filesystem.Loader",
                        "django.template.loaders.app_directories.Loader",
                    ],
                )
            ],
        },
    }
]

The builtin is the part that is easy to miss. Adding "template_partials" to INSTALLED_APPS sets up the loader and nothing else, so the page's template fails to parse at {% partialdef %}; and a {% load partials %} in the template instead would break it again on Django 6.0, which has the tag itself and no such library. From 6.0, configure none of this. Without either, the address is a TemplateDoesNotExist. A fragment kept in a file of its own, or under another name, is one attribute, fragment_template_name, and renders on any Django. That is how the shipped page carries its form: an htmx request to a page naming no template is answered with django_spec_html/spec_form_fragment.html, with nothing to configure on any Django.

Which requests get the fragment. A request whose HX-Request header is true, unless it is boosted (HX-Boosted) or a history restore (HX-History-Restore-Request): a boosted link or form swaps the whole body, and a history restore after a cache miss needs the whole page back, so both get the page. The view reads django-htmx's request.htmx where its middleware set it and the three headers where it did not, so a project with django-htmx and one without get the same answer; it imports nothing from django-htmx. The rule is one method, wants_fragment(request), to override. Every answer sets Vary on those three headers, the page's included, since one URL answers two bodies and a cache keyed on fewer would hand a fragment to a page load.

What the fragment answers, outcome by outcome:

  • GET renders the form fragment, unbound, so an hx-get can load the form into a dialog.
  • A refusal the page re-renders is the form fragment, bound the same way and from the same context, at 200 where the page answers 4xx: htmx swaps no 4xx response by default, so a refusal answered at one would land nowhere. The table above has each row, and the outcome stays in the body and in the map.
  • A success is fragment_success(result). Where the fragment template defines spec-result, that is rendered in place at 200, and HX-Trigger: spec-succeeded names an event for the rest of the page to listen for. Its context is result, view, spec and extra_context, and no form, since the post's form is done with. Otherwise it is HX-Redirect to get_success_url(result), at 200 and never a 302: an XHR follows a 302 itself and would swap the next page into the form. The URL is encoded and checked as the page's redirect is, so a path outside ASCII arrives as the page's Location would, and an unsafe scheme such as javascript: raises DisallowedRedirect in both modes. The answer passes back through the host's middleware like any other, so a cookie set for the request, such as the session a sign-in rotates, is set on it. Override the method for HX-Location, or a 204 carrying HX-Trigger.
  • A denial is raised in both modes alike, for the host's handlers.

A template with no fragment at the address answers htmx with Django's TemplateDoesNotExist naming it - spec_form.html#spec-form, or the fragment_template_name that is missing - and never with the page instead, which swapped into a form's target would nest a second layout inside it.

No htmx header reaches the spec. The mode is read only after the outcome is decided, to choose the wrapper: the arguments are the form's fields and the route's kwargs, and dispatch is called the same way in both modes. So a spec cannot branch on the mode, and its outcome on the page and in a fragment is one outcome. One header is read before dispatch, HX-Trigger-Name, and only to stop a post committing on a page that names its commit button.

A denial is the host's to answer, for htmx too. The view raises PermissionDenied and Http404 in both modes, and a handler answering an htmx request with a bare 403 shows nothing, since htmx swaps no 4xx. htmx acts on HX-Redirect and HX-Refresh whatever the status, so a handler can keep the 403 and still send the visitor somewhere:

def handler403(request: HttpRequest, exception: Exception | None = None) -> HttpResponse:
    """The host's 403: a page for a browser, and for htmx a header saying where to go."""
    if request.headers.get("HX-Request") != "true":
        response = permission_denied(request, exception)
    else:
        # htmx swaps no 4xx body, but it acts on these two headers whatever
        # the status, so the 403 keeps its status and still reaches the visitor.
        response = HttpResponse(status=403)
        if request.user.is_authenticated:
            # Signed in and still refused: reload. A page that refuses this
            # principal on GET answers the reload with its 403 page; a denial
            # only the operation raises does not recur on GET, so the reload
            # shows the form again, empty.
            response["HX-Refresh"] = "true"
        else:
            # Sign in, then come back to the page the form is on.
            here = request.headers.get("HX-Current-URL", request.get_full_path())
            response["HX-Redirect"] = redirect_to_login(here).url
    # One URL, two answers: a cache must not hand one to the other.
    patch_vary_headers(response, ("HX-Request",))
    return response

Defined in the root URLconf as handler403, it sends an anonymous visitor to sign in and back to the page the form is on, and reloads the page for a signed-in one. The reload answers with the 403 page only where the page itself refuses on GET: the spec's class-level check, or the object-level check on the row the route names. A denial only the operation raises, from inside the service, does not recur on GET, so the reload shows the form again, empty, and what was typed is gone; a host whose services refuse that way answers those in the form instead, by raising a ServiceError. The view's Vary never reaches a denial, which is raised rather than answered, so the handler sets its own on HX-Request, since it answers the two kinds of request differently.

docs.title: A post that does not commit
docs.text:
A form that refreshes a dependent choice, adds a row or searches posts without meaning to run the operation. commit_button names the submit button whose post commits, and every other post re-renders the form. It is None by default, and then every post commits, as a page that does not set it always has.

class AddEditionForm(forms.Form):
    # Choosing an author posts the form again, through htmx where it is
    # loaded, so the books offered below are theirs.
    author = forms.ModelChoiceField(
        queryset=Author.objects.all(),
        widget=forms.Select(
            attrs={
                "hx-post": "",
                "hx-trigger": "change",
                "hx-target": "closest form",
                "hx-swap": "outerHTML",
            }
        ),
    )
    book = forms.ModelChoiceField(queryset=Book.objects.none())
    number = forms.IntegerField(min_value=1)

    def __init__(self, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        # The books of the author the post names, and none until it names
        # one: a string from the page's post, the number itself in the form
        # the Validator binds to the coerced arguments.
        author = self.data.get(self.add_prefix("author"))
        if str(author).isdigit():
            self.fields["book"].queryset = Book.objects.filter(author_id=author)


def add_edition(*, data: dict[str, Any]) -> Edition:
    return Edition.objects.create(book=data["book"], number=data["number"])


add_edition_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=add_edition,
    permissions=[IsSignedIn()],
    validator=FormValidator(AddEditionForm),
)

The URLconf routes it as editions/new/, with commit_button="add", and its form is a file of its own, so it renders on any Django:

<form method="post" hx-post="" hx-swap="outerHTML">{% csrf_token %}
  {{ form }}
  <button name="add">Add the edition</button>
  <button name="refresh" formnovalidate>Show their books</button>
</form>

Choosing an author posts the form, through htmx where it is loaded, and "Show their books" does the same without it. Neither carries add, so neither runs the operation; the form comes back with the books of the author posted, and "Add the edition" commits. A book by another author is refused on that post, since the Validator's form is narrowed by the same post.

Which posts commit, decided by one method, commits(request), to override for another rule, such as two buttons that both commit:

  • The post's data must carry the button's name. A browser posts the name and value of the submit button that was pressed and of no other, with or without JavaScript. htmx does the same for a form it submits, and posts no button's name for a request a control issues itself, such as the author picker's hx-post.
  • Under htmx 2, HX-Trigger-Name can stop a commit, never make one. It names the element the request came from: the form, whose name is never posted, or a control, whose own value always is. A header naming a key the post carries, other than the button, is another control's request, and does not commit even where the button's name reached the data some other way, such as an inherited hx-vals. A form's own name, or no header at all, leaves the decision to the data, which is what decides for every client: a browser and htmx alike post the pressed button's name.
  • Enter presses the first submit button in the form, so put the commit button first, as the template above does; a refresh button placed before it would turn Enter into a refresh. Give a refresh button formnovalidate, so the browser posts the form with its required fields still blank.

What a post that does not commit renders is the page GET renders, with the form bound to the post:

  • It is admitted and finds its target as GET does, so a principal the spec refuses is refused, and the context carries target, the count of a set, target_display and unavailable as GET's does.
  • The form is built through form_kwargs like every other form the page builds, bound to the post, so a choice its constructor narrows - by a keyword, or by a value posted - is narrowed again.
  • Nothing is dispatched and nothing validated: the form shows the values posted and no error, and a required field left blank is not called required. asked_fields are held back, as on GET.
  • The context carries refreshed, True, for a template that needs to tell; it is absent from every other render.
  • The page answers 200, and an htmx request the form's fragment at 200.

commit_button is checked at as_view(): None, or a non-empty string that names no field of the form, since a field is posted by every submit and could not say which one commits.

docs.title: A success message
docs.text:
success_message is sent through django.contrib.messages on every success: the page's redirect, the HX-Redirect and the result fragment alike. It is formatted as Django's SuccessMessageMixin formats its own, % with the form's cleaned data, so "Edition %(number)s added." above reads the number posted, as the form cleaned it. The cleaned data is the result's data, what the Validator's form handed the service; on a partial page a field left blank is not in it.

get_success_message(result) answers it, to override for a message that reads what the operation returned:

class AddBookThenSayWhich(SpecFormView):
    def get_success_message(self, result: DispatchResult) -> str:
        return f"Book {result.value.pk} added."
  • Without the messages middleware it is skipped, and never raises Django's MessageFailure: a message needs the store the middleware puts on the request, which the app installed alone does not, and the write has already committed.
  • A refusal, a confirmation page and a post that does not commit send none. The message is sent once the operation has run.
  • An empty message, the default, sends nothing.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text: Everything below is exported from django_spec_html directly, and from the subpackage it is listed under. Import from the package root in application code; the subpackage paths are where each name is defined. Kernel names these views read - ServiceSpec, dispatch, the refusals - are documented on the kernel's site.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
This package defines none. The argument reader reads one of the kernel's:

  • SERVICE_SPECS_MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH: the longest list an array parameter with no max_length of its own takes. It is the kernel's key, read by the kernel, and keeps its name here. See how long a list may be.

docs.title: SpecFormView
docs.text:
Bases: SpecPageBase

A ServiceSpec validated by a form, served as the page a person fills that form in on.

The spec's Validator must be a FormValidator, and its form class is the page's form:

urlpatterns = [
    path(
        "books/new/",
        SpecFormView.as_view(spec=add_book_spec, success_url=reverse_lazy("books")),
    ),
]

GET renders template_name with an unbound form under form, beside view and spec: the names Django's FormView uses, with extra_context merged in as Django's ContextMixin does. The spec's class-level permission check runs first, through authorize, so a page is never offered to a principal the post would refuse.

The page's template is optional. template_name is django_spec_html/spec_form.html by default, a template this package ships: a plain document with no stylesheet, script or htmx attribute, holding the target pane, an unmet affordance's reason with the form disabled, and the form - its errors, a question's message and the field it asks for, and a submit button posting commit_button's name where one is set - inside a POST form with its token. It is found as any app's templates are, so a project lists django_spec_html in INSTALLED_APPS with APP_DIRS on, and as_view() refuses a page rendering it that no template engine finds. Its form is a file of its own, django_spec_html/spec_form_fragment.html, which the page includes and an htmx request is answered with, on every Django. Override either file the Django way, with one of the same name in a template directory found first, or django_spec_html/base.html, the document every shipped page extends; or set template_name to a page of the project's own.

An update's page shows the row it updates. Every GET then finds its target as dispatch would, through resolve_target on the route's kwargs, coerced as a post's are: the row or set a target selector resolves, or None for a create. A check refusing it - the object-level check on a row, the scope check on a set or on None - raises PermissionDenied, as the post would be refused; a missing row or a selector's ServiceNotFound raises Http404; and a route value the spec's parameters refuse raises Django's BadRequest. The form shows a row's values for its own fields: a ModelForm of the row's model is built on a copy of it, as the Validator binds one, and any other form takes the row's values for the enabled fields it names as its initial. So a file the row holds is shown, with the clear checkbox an optional file's ClearableFileInput offers beside it. A create, a collection target and a missing row allow_none lets through show an empty form.

POST starts as GET does: the route first, then that check, and only then is the form built from the post. A refused post is answered with the page again, and dispatch's shape check comes before its own permission check, so without it a principal the spec refuses would be shown the page - every row a choice field lists, and extra_context - by posting a malformed form, and a form whose constructor reads rows would read them for that principal. The Grant it returns goes to dispatch, so the class-level check runs once.

Then the post finds its target, as GET does, before the form is built or read, so the form a refused post re-renders is built on the row as the page's was, its held file and clear checkbox shown. The target answers before the shape check: the object-level and scope checks and a missing row refuse a malformed post as they would a well-formed one, rather than dispatch re-rendering the page for a principal the row refuses. Dispatch is handed the target and the grant resolve_target returns, so it looks nothing up again and asks no check twice. A route value the target's reads refuse is left to dispatch, whose one refusal carries it beside the form's own.

POST binds the form to the post and reads the arguments through its own widgets - a checkbox is True or False, a multi-select a list - because that is how Django reads a form, and a flat reading refuses a checkbox's "on". Only the form's fields are read, so the CSRF token and a named submit button never become arguments, and a disabled field is not read at all, as the form ignores what is posted for it. A field left blank is absent, as it is to the form. A number, date or date-time the field reads in one of its input formats - 10/25/2006, a localized 12,50 - is sent on in the form the shape check reads, through the field's own to_python, so the shape check never refuses what the form accepts. The URL kwargs are merged last, so the route wins a clash, as in request_arguments. Each is an argument, so the spec declares each one: a kwarg it does not is the host's misconfiguration, raised as ImproperlyConfigured under either unknown_arguments policy rather than answered as a refused post. Then dispatch:

  • A success redirects to get_success_url(result): success_url through Django's resolve_url by default, so a reverse_lazy or a URL name works, and a subclass overrides it to read the result.
  • A refusal of the arguments - InvalidArguments, or a ServiceValidationError - re-renders the bound form at 400 with the refusal placed on it by add_argument_errors. A service's string or list detail is about the whole form.
  • Any other refusal re-renders it with the message as a non-field error: ServiceConflict at 409, any other ServiceError at 422, UnsupportedMediaType at 415, any other DispatchError at 400. The statuses are error_response's, read from the one map, so a client reading a refused post - Turbo, which will not render a failed post answered 200 - reads it the same way.
  • A question, AdditionalInputRequired, re-renders it at 422, the message as a non-field error, as the confirmation page below.
  • NotPermitted and PrincipalUnavailable raise Django's PermissionDenied, and a not-found result or ServiceNotFound raises Http404, for the host's own 403 and 404 pages.

The confirmation page is an AdditionalInputRequired rendered. Its schema is checked first by the kernel's check_requested_input, with the call's seeds, so a question no route could hear answered - a key no parameter declares, one a seed fills, a shape a transport cannot render, a type the parameter refuses - raises ImproperlyConfigured on the page and in the fragment alike, and is never rendered. Then the bound form is re-rendered with every value posted, and the context carries requested_input: the message, the schema, and the fields, the form's bound fields the schema names. The page builds no widget from a schema. The answer is a field the spec's form declares, an optional BooleanField whose absent box cleans to False, and asked_fields holds it back until a question names it: it is taken out of the form each GET and every other refusal renders, so it posts nothing of its own, and shown empty when asked, so a yes is never carried over to a question asked again. A key no field declares is asked by the message alone. The target is found and a set counted again for the post that asked, so the page says what it found then.

Two wrappers, one outcome. The view decides what a request ends in once - a success, or the refusal's Outcome - and only then reads who asked, to choose how to answer it. Every request gets the page above unless wants_fragment says htmx asked for less, and then the same outcome is answered as a fragment, at the same URL:

  • The form renders get_fragment_template_names() where the page renders template_name, from the same context: on GET, and on every refusal the page re-renders, at 200 rather than the page's 4xx, since htmx swaps no 4xx by default. A shipped page's is its fragment file. For a page of the project's own the default address is <template_name>#spec-form, a {% partialdef %} inside the page's own template, which Django 6.0 resolves; below it, django-template-partials does, with its tag named in TEMPLATES as a builtin ("builtins": ["template_partials.templatetags.partials"]) and its loader around the project's. A template with no fragment at the address is Django's TemplateDoesNotExist naming it, never the page, which swapped into a form's target would nest a second layout inside it.
  • A success is fragment_success(result): HX-Redirect to get_success_url(result), or the spec-result fragment in place.
  • A denial is raised in both modes alike, for the host's handlers.

Both wrappers set Vary on the three headers the choice reads. No htmx header reaches dispatch: the arguments are the form's fields and the route's kwargs whichever wrapper answers, so a spec cannot tell the two apart. One header is read before dispatch, HX-Trigger-Name, and only to stop a post committing, below.

A post that does not commit. A form that refreshes a dependent choice, adds a row or searches posts without meaning to run the operation. commit_button names the submit button whose post commits; None, the default, commits every post. Once set, commits(request) decides: a post whose data does not carry that name, or an htmx request whose HX-Trigger-Name names another control the post carries, is the page GET renders, admitted and with its target, its affordances and asked_fields held back as GET's are, but with the form bound to the post and built through form_kwargs as every form is, so a choice its constructor narrows by a posted value is narrowed again. Nothing is dispatched and nothing validated: the form shows no error, and the context carries refreshed, absent from every other render. It answers 200 on the page, and the form's fragment at 200 under htmx.

A success message. success_message, where it is set, is sent through django.contrib.messages on every success - the redirect, the HX-Redirect and the result fragment alike - formatted by get_success_message(result), % with the form's cleaned data as Django's SuccessMessageMixin formats it. Without the messages middleware it is skipped, and never raises MessageFailure. A refusal, a confirmation page and a post that does not commit send none.

The request is read through the same attributes and hooks as SpecView's, checked by the same code in http/utils.py: route_kwargs says which URL kwargs fill which parameters; get_pool_seeds(request), asked once per request, answers the seeds the class-level check, the target's lookup and its object-level or scope check, the form's form_kwargs, the affordances and dispatch are handed, each resolving only the seeds it names; and get_server_arguments(request) answers the binding, laid over the route's arguments before the target is found and over the post's before dispatch. A field of the page's form the binding binds renders disabled with the server's value, and one it withholds disabled and empty, so the post never reads it. A named seed is resolved again at each step that names it, since a Grant carries no values: a resolver answering a fresh object answers each step a different one.

The page's form is the Validator's, built with what its form_kwargs answers, through the kernel's form_keywords: on GET, on a refused post and for its own validation below, with the principal, the request's seeds, the row the post acts on and the request's one call context, the very dict dispatch is then handed. So a form whose __init__ takes a keyword - a queryset scoped by a tenant - is served, and the page's form offers the choices the Validator's accepts.

One call context per request: a plain dict the page creates for the request and hands, as the same object, to every kernel call it makes - the class-level check, the target's lookup and its checks, the affordances, the form's keywords and dispatch - so a check, a condition or the service declaring call_context reads what an earlier stage put there.

GET asks the spec's affordances once the target is found: the callable conditions always, through the kernel's unmet_operation_affordance on a pool built from the call's seeds, and, with none of those unmet and a row to ask about, the conditions on the row, as dispatch asks them. The first unmet Affordance is in the context as unavailable, for a template to read its code and reason; it is absent when every condition is met. The POST is unchanged, and dispatch's 409 stays the authority. A refused post's context carries code, the ActionUnavailable's, for a refusal carrying one, as error_response puts it in the JSON body; it is absent for every other.

The page shows its target, on GET and on every refused post it re-renders, in the context beside the form: target is the row an instance selector found, or the set a collection_selector_spec resolved, and it is absent for a create and for a missing row allow_none lets through. A set comes with target_count, how many rows it held, and target_counted_at, when it was counted (django.utils.timezone.now()), so a template says "117 rows matched at 14:02" rather than promising a number the confirming post may not find. An empty set is no refusal: its scope check is asked, and the page counts 0. A queryset is counted by a COUNT on a fresh clone, never by reading its rows; the post re-runs the service on the set as it is then, and a refused one is counted again. A successful post counts nothing.

target_display is the target as a person reads it, on a page that sets display_target. It is off by default: an Output describes what the operation returns, which need not be its target, so a page presents its target only where it says the Output describes it. On, the target is presented through the spec's presenter - its own, or its output selector's - with the context dispatch hands it, projected by the kernel's project_payload, and with every HANDLE dropped as well as every HIDDEN one. A row's is a dict of its fields, with label, the value of the field marked LABEL, beside them where there is one, and pairs, the same fields as name and value in order, for a template to loop over, since fields.items reads a field named items; a set's is a list of those, one per row, for at most target_display_limit rows, read in one query. as_view() refuses a page displaying its target whose spec has no Output, whose Output marks none of its own fields with a FieldMarking, or whose markings the kernel's projection refuses, such as two labels. Whether the Output describes the target's rows is known only once one is presented: an Output that does not raises on the page's first request, which is the cost of turning the display on.

A refusal of the arguments shows every error in one post. Beside an InvalidArguments, the page's own form - built as the Validator's is, with the same keywords - is validated too, and the refusal is placed beside what it found, never twice. So after a shape-check refusal - a required field left blank, a date that does not parse - the form's further checks, a length, clean() or uniqueness, answer in the same post rather than the next. It is validated as the Validator validates its own, under the kernel's clean_held_to_their_columns, so a value no column holds - a key past 64 bits - is refused in the field's words and never reaches the database driver. A post whose route the target's reads refuse never found its row, so its form is not judged as one and carries the refusal alone. Any other refusal is no verdict on the arguments - a conflict, a service's own rule, an unavailable action - and the page's form carries it alone, validated no further.

A partial spec's page renders no HTML required attribute, so the browser sends a post that leaves fields blank, and a blank field is absent: on a partial call, one the operation leaves as it is. A post with every field blank dispatches with no arguments but what a checkbox or a multi-select always sends, and is not refused. Beside a shape-check refusal, a partial page's form carries the refusal alone: its Validator takes the fields a post leaves out off its own form, and the page's form, validated whole, would call each one required.

as_view() refuses, when the URLconf is imported, a view with no ServiceSpec, a spec whose Validator is not a FormValidator, a many spec, whose list of rows no form posts, a view with no success_url that does not override get_success_url, and a commit_button that is not a button's name or is one of the form's fields.

Sync only, in this release. CSRF is the host's middleware, as for any Django view, and the template renders {% csrf_token %}.

wants_fragment(request: HttpRequest) -> bool

Whether request is answered with a fragment rather than the page.

An htmx request is, unless it is boosted or a history restore: a boosted link or form swaps the whole body, and a history restore after a cache miss needs the whole page back, so both get the page. Read from django-htmx's request.htmx where its middleware set it, and from the three headers where it did not, so a host with django-htmx and one without get the same answer. Override it for another rule; the headers every answer varies on stay these three.

Each condition, on each path, is held by its own row: test_read_from_the_headers (htmx-false, boosted, history-restore) and test_read_from_django_htmx_where_its_middleware_ran (not-htmx, boosted, history-restore), whose headers say the opposite of the details, so reading the wrong one fails it.

docs.title: commits
docs.text:
commits(request: HttpRequest) -> bool

Whether a post runs the operation, or re-renders its form with the post's values.

Every post commits while commit_button is None. Once it names a button, a post commits only when its data carries that name, which is how a browser says which submit button was pressed, with or without JavaScript; htmx 2 adds the clicked button's name and value to a form's post, and sends no button's name for a request a control of its own issued, such as a <select hx-post>.

HX-Trigger-Name, which htmx 2 sends, can only stop a commit, never make one. It names the element the request was issued from, and that element's own value is in the post when it is a control, while a form's name never is. So a header naming a key the post carries, other than the button, is another control's request, and does not commit even where something - an inherited hx-vals, a hidden input - put the button's name in the data. A form's own name in the header, or none at all, leaves the decision to the data. A value htmx had to encode is read decoded, as HX-Trigger-Name-URI-AutoEncoded says.

One branch to coverage, so each condition is held by its own test: test_a_post_without_the_button_neither_dispatches_nor_validates (the data must carry the button), test_a_trigger_naming_another_posted_control_does_not_commit (the header vetoes), test_a_trigger_that_is_the_button_itself_commits (the button issuing its own request is no other control) and test_a_trigger_naming_the_form_commits (a name the post does not carry is no control). Override it for another rule, such as two buttons that both commit.

docs.text:
get_fragment_template_names() -> list[str]

The templates a fragment's form renders: fragment_template_name, or each page's #spec-form.

The default addresses a {% partialdef spec-form %} inside the page's template, so turning htmx on is a template change. The tag and the #name address are Django 6.0's. Below it they are django-template-partials', configured in TEMPLATES with its tag as a builtin, "builtins": ["template_partials.templatetags.partials"], and its loader around the project's: installed as an app alone, it wraps the loader and the page fails to parse at {% partialdef %}. Without either, the default is a TemplateDoesNotExist naming it.

A page this package ships is the exception: its form is a file of its own, which the page includes, so the fragment is that file on every Django (test_the_shipped_page_s_fragment_is_its_own_file). A project overriding a shipped page's file keeps the shipped fragment, and overrides the fragment's file to change the form.

docs.title: fragment_success
docs.text:
fragment_success(result: DispatchResult) -> HttpResponse

A success, answered to the htmx request that posted it.

Where the fragment template defines a spec-result fragment, that is rendered in place at 200, and HX-Trigger names spec-succeeded for the rest of the page to listen for. Its context is the view's - view, spec and extra_context - with result in it, and no form, since the post's form is done with. Otherwise HX-Redirect to get_success_url(result), at 200 and never a 302: an XHR follows a 302 itself and would swap the next page into the form. The URL is encoded and checked as the page's redirect is, so a path outside ASCII reaches the browser as the page's Location would, and an unsafe scheme raises DisallowedRedirect in both modes.

The answer passes back through the host's middleware like any other, so a cookie it sets for the request - the session a sign-in rotates, a message - is set on it. Override it to answer another way, with HX-Location, say, or a 204 carrying HX-Trigger.

docs.title: SpecConfirmView
docs.text:
Bases: SpecPageBase

A ServiceSpec with no Validator, served as a page showing what it acts on and a button.

For an operation a person confirms rather than fills in - withdrawing a row, archiving a set - whose every argument the server answers: the route, a pool seed, a kwargs provider or server_arguments. The spec declares validator=None:

urlpatterns = [
    path(
        "books/<int:pk>/withdraw/",
        SpecConfirmView.as_view(
            spec=withdraw_book_spec,
            success_url=reverse_lazy("books"),
            route_kwargs=("pk",),
        ),
    ),
]

What it shares with SpecFormView is everything but the form: the principal admitted by the class-level check before anything is shown, the target found as dispatch finds it - target, a set's target_count and target_counted_at, and target_display on a page that sets display_target - the affordances asked on GET as unavailable, commit_button, the fragment wrapper under htmx, the request hooks, success_url and success_message, each as SpecFormView documents it.

GET renders template_name with that context, beside view and spec, and no form: there is nothing to fill in, so the template renders its own <form method="post">, the CSRF token and the submit button. A key with nothing to hold is absent, as on every page, so {{ form }} is never None.

The page's template is optional, as on SpecFormView: django_spec_html/spec_confirm.html by default, which this package ships, with its button in django_spec_html/spec_confirm_fragment.html. It renders the target pane, an unmet affordance's reason with the button disabled, a refused post's errors or a question's message alone, and the button, posting commit_button's name where one is set. Found, refused at as_view() and overridden as SpecFormView's is.

POST dispatches with the route's kwargs, read by route_kwargs and coerced as a form page's are, under the binding and with the request's seeds. Nothing the post carries becomes an argument: not the CSRF token, not the button, and not a key named like a parameter, so the closed argument set holds with nothing to check. A success redirects to get_success_url(result), or under htmx answers HX-Redirect or the spec-result fragment, with success_message sent through django.contrib.messages where its middleware runs.

A refused post is the confirmation page again, at the status of the one map - 400 for an argument refusal, 409 for a conflict or an unavailable action, 422 for any other service refusal - or as the fragment at 200 under htmx, and needs no messages app. Its context carries errors, every message the refusal holds as a list of strings, a message about a parameter prefixed with its path ("pk: Enter a whole number."), and code for a refusal carrying one. A denial is raised for the host's 403 or 404 page, as on any page.

A question is shown, and cannot be answered here. A service raising AdditionalInputRequired re-renders the page at 422, its schema first checked by the kernel's check_requested_input, with requested_input - the message and the schema - and the message in errors. The page builds no control from a schema, and no post is read for an answer, so a confirming post is asked again. An operation that asks a person something mid-flight declares a form that holds the answer, and is served by SpecFormView with its asked_fields.

as_view() refuses, when the URLconf is imported, a spec with a Validator - a FormValidator's is SpecFormView's to serve - and a spec demanding a parameter that nothing but a post could supply, besides everything the page base refuses. Which parameters a call demands is the kernel's answer, through bind_arguments on a call carrying nothing, and each must be supplied by the route - a parameter route_kwargs names a kwarg into, since the URL pattern is not known when as_view() runs - by a seed the declared pool_seeds registers, as server_owned_keys reads them, or by a value server_arguments binds.

get_success_message(result: DispatchResult) -> str

success_message formatted with the target: "%(target)s was withdrawn.".

docs.text:
Bases: SpecPageBase

A many ServiceSpec validated by a form, served as a formset of that form, one form a row.

A many spec takes a list of rows under its many_argument, and the kernel validates the call per row: the shape check and the Validator run on each row, and a refusal is addressed by the row's index. So the page is a formset of the spec's form class, and the formset is this page's alone: FormValidator never sees one. The spec's Validator must be a FormValidator:

urlpatterns = [
    path(
        "books/new/",
        SpecFormSetView.as_view(spec=add_books_spec, success_url=reverse_lazy("books")),
    ),
]

GET renders template_name with an unbound formset under formset, beside view and spec, once the spec's class-level check admits the principal, as SpecFormView's page does. The formset shows extra blank forms, after the spec's many_min_length forms, which a person must fill; and never more than many_max_length. The template renders {{ formset }} - its management form included - inside a POST form with its token.

The page's template is optional, as on SpecFormView: django_spec_html/spec_form_set.html by default, which this package ships, with its formset in django_spec_html/spec_form_set_fragment.html. It renders the management form, the formset's non-form errors, each form as a fieldset of its own with its errors, and the submit button posting commit_button's name where one is set, then the add_button, which skips the browser's checks since its post commits nothing. No target pane. Found, refused at as_view() and overridden as SpecFormView's is.

No target pane. A many spec declares no target selector, which the kernel refuses when the spec is built, so there is no row or set to show: the context carries no target, target_count or target_display, and display_target is refused at as_view().

Every form is built as the Validator builds a row's, with what its form_kwargs answers, through the kernel's form_keywords: asked once per request, with the principal, the request's seeds and its one call context, and handed to every form as the formset's form_kwargs. There is no target to hand it, so the answer is the same for every row, and asking once is asking what each row would be asked. A form whose __init__ takes a keyword is served.

POST reads each form the formset bound, in the formset's order, as SpecFormView reads its one form - through its own widgets, a blank field absent, a disabled one not read - and sends the rows as one list under many_argument. The route's kwargs are read and coerced once for the call, beside the list, never inside a row. The management form's keys are the formset's, and never become arguments, as the CSRF token never does. An extra form left unchanged sends no row: the form Django would let through empty is not sent, so a page offering three blank forms posts only those a person filled in. The first many_min_length forms are sent however they are left, so the kernel refuses a row left blank where the spec requires it. A post whose management form is missing or tampered with is refused before dispatch, in Django's own words, at 400.

A refusal is split back onto the forms. One addressed to row i of the list lands on the form that posted it, through add_argument_errors, so a dropped blank form shifts nothing; one about the list as a whole - its length, a message about the rows together - and one about a route value land on the formset's non_form_errors(), a route value prefixed with its name as on the single page. Beside an InvalidArguments each sent form is validated too, under the kernel's clean_held_to_their_columns, so every row's own checks answer in the same post; on a partial spec, and for any other refusal, the forms carry the refusal alone. Any other refusal's message is a non-form error, at the status SpecFormView answers it with.

A question is answered by its message alone. An AdditionalInputRequired is checked by the kernel's check_requested_input as on every page, so a schema no route could hear answered - a key declared only inside a row among them - raises ImproperlyConfigured and is never rendered. Then the formset is re-rendered at 422 with the message as a non-form error and requested_input, its message and schema, in the context, with no fields: a many call's top level is the list and the spec's reads, which no form declares, and the page builds no widget from a schema, so a once-for-the-call confirmation is not built on this page.

A post that does not commit, the fragment wrapper, the request hooks and denials are SpecFormView's, by the same code: see that page. With commit_button set, add_button names a second submit button whose post is the page again with one more form, bound to everything posted, never past many_max_length, and nothing dispatched.

A success message is success_message formatted with {"count": n}, the number of rows the call carried, so "%(count)d books were added." reads the post's own count. The single page formats with the cleaned data, and a many call's is a list, which % with a name cannot read. Override get_success_message to read result.data, the rows' cleaned data, or result.value.

as_view() refuses, when the URLconf is imported, a spec whose Validator is not a FormValidator, a spec that is not many, a view displaying its target, an extra that is not a non-negative int, and an add_button that is not a button's name, that is set without a commit_button, or that is the commit_button; and either button named under the formset's form- prefix, which every post carries.

docs.text:
Bases: ModelAdmin

A ModelAdmin offering each spec in spec_actions as an action, served by the spec's own page.

Mixed in ahead of admin.ModelAdmin, or of any subclass of it, with one SpecAction per operation:

@admin.register(Book)
class BookAdmin(SpecActionsMixin, admin.ModelAdmin):
    spec_actions = (
        SpecAction("withdraw", withdraw_book_spec, "Withdraw", parameter="pk"),
        SpecAction("publish", publish_books_spec, "Publish", parameter="pks"),
    )

Which kind of action is the spec's target's answer. A spec with an instance_selector_spec is an object action: a link among the change page's object tools, to <object_id>/actions/<name>/, whose object_id fills the selector's parameter through the page's route_kwargs, unquoted as the admin quotes it. A spec with a collection_selector_spec is a changelist action: an entry in the action dropdown, which redirects to actions/<name>/ with the selected rows' primary keys in the query string, repeated under parameter. The page binds them to that parameter as server_arguments, read from the query string on GET and on the post the page sends back to its own URL, so nothing posted stands in for the selection; and the collection selector still decides the set, so a key it does not answer is not acted on.

The admin's scope comes first, as for its own actions and its change page: a page is served only to a principal holding the admin's view or change permission, the row's on an object action, and acts only on rows in the admin's get_queryset(). An object action's row outside it is a 404, and a changelist action's selection is narrowed to it before it is bound, so a key outside it never reaches the selector. Within that scope the spec's own checks run, and its selector decides the set.

Each page is the spec's own: SpecFormView for a spec validating with a FormValidator, SpecConfirmView for one with none, built once when the admin is registered, so as_view() refuses then what it refuses of any page. Its URL is added by get_urls() ahead of the admin's own, wrapped in admin_site.admin_view(), so only a signed-in staff member the site admits reaches it; the page then admits the principal by the admin's permission and the spec's own checks, as on any route, and answers the rest with the host's 403 page. Its templates, django_spec_html/admin/spec_form.html and django_spec_html/admin/spec_confirm.html, extend admin/base_site.html with the admin's breadcrumbs and title around the very fragment the shipped page includes, so an htmx request is answered with that fragment, as on any page. A success returns to the row's change page or to the changelist, with the page's success_message among the admin's messages.

Offered only to a principal both admit. The object-tools link and the dropdown entry are shown only where the kernel's authorize, the spec's class-level check, admits the request's principal, asked with the page's own seeds and call context, and the admin's view or change permission does too. The admin's model permissions say nothing about the spec's, so they are not the whole gate: the spec's checks are asked as well, and the page asks both again, the object-level ones included, on every request. An entry not offered is not in get_actions(), which the changelist reads again on the post that runs an action, so posting its name runs nothing.

The change page is rendered from django_spec_html/admin/change_form.html, which extends admin/change_form.html and lists the links ahead of the admin's own tools: a ModelAdmin setting a change_form_template of its own extends that template to keep them.

ImproperlyConfigured is raised when the admin is registered for a declaration that is not a SpecAction, a name that is not a slug, is used twice or is one of the admin's own URL names, a label that does not format with the model's names, a spec that is not a ServiceSpec, a many spec, a spec with no target, a parameter its target selector does not read or, on a changelist action, one that is not an array, and a page_kwargs key the mixin answers for.
